theorem.title: Duality Generation
theorem.para: Let C = (ℒ, ℛ) be a sequent calculus whose rules are presented in bilateral Gentzen form. Define two operations on calculi:

listitem.para: Left-dualization δL: for each connective, exchange its left-introduction rule with the left-right mirror image of its right-introduction rule, leaving all other rules unchanged.
Right-dualization δR: for each connective, exchange its right-introduction rule with the left-right mirror image of its left-introduction rule, leaving all other rules unchanged.

theorem.para: Then δL and δR are both involutions, they commute, and the group G = ⟨δL, δR⟩ is isomorphic to a quotient of ℤ/2ℤ × ℤ/2ℤ. The orbit {C, δL(C), δR(C), δL(δR(C))} has cardinality at most 4; it has cardinality exactly 4 when C is not a fixed point of either δL or δR.

proof.para: That each operation is an involution follows by inspection: applying δL twice to any rule restores it to its original form, since the exchange is its own inverse. Commutativity holds because δL and δR act on disjoint families of rules: the former on the left-introduction rules for each connective, the latter on the right-introduction rules. Rules in neither affected family are unchanged by both operations, and the order in which the exchanges are performed is therefore immaterial. The orbit cardinality claim is a standard consequence of the orbit-stabilizer theorem applied to an action of ℤ/2ℤ × ℤ/2ℤ on a set: an orbit has size equal to the index of the stabilizer of any of its elements, and the stabilizer of C is trivial if and only if C is a fixed point of neither generator.
